title: Use the reference well
scenario: A client loves the palette and window light of a reference photo of a restaurant and wants an illustration that feels like it — but in a different room, with the client's own layout. You are writing the generation instruction.
task: Which instruction makes honest, effective use of the reference?

options.text: Illustrate this exact photo — same room, same layout — in a painted style.
options.feedback: That copies the composition you were asked to replace, and “exact” is not something the model can honour anyway.

options.text: Using the reference for palette, light and texture only — warm terracotta and cream, soft window light from the left, visible watercolour grain — illustrate a different dining room with the client's own layout.
options.feedback: The attributes you actually want are named; the composition is explicitly yours. Renderable, honest and reusable as a brief.

options.text: Make an illustration in the style of the photo, very similar and beautiful.
options.feedback: “Similar” and “beautiful” transfer nothing specific — palette, light and texture stay in the lottery.

hints: Which attributes do you actually want from the photo — and which do you need to leave behind?
An instruction works when every part of it is renderable: name the palette, the light, the texture, the new layout.
explanation: References transfer best when decomposed: palette, light, texture, mood. The winning instruction names exactly those attributes and states what stays new — the room and the layout. “Exact photo” copies what you must change; “similar and beautiful” names nothing. Decomposing also gives you the credit line for free: inspired by the reference for palette and light, authored by you everywhere else.
